Q: Can I test my Codename One app on my iOS device for free? A:

Yes, if you have a Mac with Xcode.

Generate the local Xcode project from the Codename One Maven project, open the generated workspace in Xcode, sign in with a free Apple Account, and select your Personal Team for signing. Xcode can then install the app on your personal device without jailbreaking.

Free provisioning has significant limits: profiles expire after seven days, the number of registered apps and devices is restricted, and some capabilities require paid membership (Apple membership, not Codename One). You must rebuild and reinstall after the profile expires.

Codename One cloud builds and the Certificate Wizard use normal Apple development/distribution signing assets, so this free path is primarily a local-Xcode workflow. App Store distribution still requires Apple Developer Program membership.

Original reply below:

You need a certificate from Apple to test on a device without using xcode and we can't realistically provide a way around it.

Getting a certificate for free from Apple is a different thing. Educational institutes usually have access to an educational apple developer account that allows you to do just that for free so if you are a student or know a student you can get access to one of those and use it to test your app on your device for free.

Q: What does the “JS” instruction do in x86 assembly? A: 
cmp %al, %cl
js  ...

This cmp instruction, as written in the AT&T syntax, compares the %al and %cl registers to each other. The comparison is made by subtracting the source operand from the destination operand. And because this is AT&T, the source operand is the leftmost operand (so %al) and the destination operand is the rightmost operand (so %cl). Thus the CPU calculates %cl - %al. None of these registers gets modified during the operation.
Both these registers are byte-sized, therefore the temporary result is also considered a byte. Whenever the CPU sees a byte, it considers the eighth bit (so bit 7) as the sign bit of that value. Only if this particular bit is in the set state (holding a 1), will the CPU raise its sign flag SF, part of the EFLAGS register.
Finally, if the SF is set, the js ... instruction will perform the jump. If the SF is not set then the execution just continues sequentially.

Also, what happens if %cl is 0 ?

With a zero in the %cl destination register, the outcome will depend on the value in the %al source register.

  • For all %al = [1,128] the temporary byte-sized value that the CPU calculates will result in a negative number and so the jump is taken.
  • For all %al = {0,[129,255]} the temporary byte-sized value that the CPU calculates will result in a non-negative number and so the jump is not taken.

And what would happen if %al were 0 ?

Then no matter the value in %cl the temporary byte-sized value that the CPU calculates (which is %cl - %al ergo %cl - 0) will result in the value that %cl already holds. Therefore the jump would be taken only if %cl itself were negative. But if that really is our intent then we'd normally be using the test instruction: test %cl, %cl js .... (This alleviates the need for a zero-holding second register to compare with).

Q: Game in Codename One A:

The Windows Phone discussion below is historical. Windows Phone is gone, and Codename One’s former UWP target was retired in 2026 (replaced with native win32 target).

Codename One now has a dedicated, GPU-accelerated gaming API. It includes GameView, scenes, sprites, sprite sheets, animated sprites, pollable input, low-latency sound and Box2D physics. The visual Game Builder supports 2D, board/isometric and 3D levels.

Therefore Codename One is now a viable option for many 2D games and some portable 3D games. The gaming and Game Builder APIs are still relatively new, so a demanding game should benchmark its real scenes and target devices before committing.

For a sprite-based game, start with GameView, Scene, SpriteSheet and AnimatedSprite, or generate a scene using:

mvn cn1:create-game-scene -DclassName=com.example.MyScene
mvn cn1:gamebuilder

See original answer below:

Codename One probably isn't the right answer for you.

The Windows Phone port for 7.5 was based on XNA but since MS effectively killed that off we had to abandon that approach and MS didn't provide any alternative (Direct X without widgets isn't an alternative). So graphics on Windows Phone are currently drawn in a relatively in-efficient way which might work for a card game but not if you need faster performance.

Android/iOS performance should be good but Windows Phone will probably under perform until MS resolves this use case.

Codename One wasn't designed as a game platform initially so it doesn't have sprites and other game mainstays but it does have components and other elements you can use. See my article for SDJ on creating a game with Codename One.

Q: How Does a Codename One Update "Work" A:

The answer originally described the retired Ant/IDE-plugin workflow. Current Codename One projects are Maven projects.

The framework and Maven plugin versions are declared by cn1.version and cn1.plugin.version in the project’s root pom.xml. Libraries are regular Maven dependencies. Use the generated Update Codename One target or run:

mvn cn1:update
Project tools now have their own Maven goals, including:
mvn cn1:settings
mvn cn1:certificatewizard
mvn cn1:guibuilder

There is no build.xml update prompt and no separate “Update Client Libs” step in a modern project.

By default, a cloud build uses the current Codename One release. Where the account permits it, a build can instead be pinned to an eligible released version or sent against master for verification. You can use versioned builds where applicable with the build servers.

Original answer below:

Codename One is comprised of several different pieces and an update usually means we update only one of them. At a high level there are really just 2 major types of updates: libraries & servers.

We update libraries once every 3-5 weeks we update servers all the time (sometimes more than once per day sometimes ever 3-4 days).

Here is a slightly more accurate overview of what it means to update Codename One:

  • Plugin & related tools - the plugin itself provides the project properties, server connectivity and designer/gui builder tools. It updates as part of the native IDE update process once every 3-5 weeks. You need to explicitly accept an update prompt from the IDE in order to get this update. Bugs in the plugin itself or features for the designer/GUI builder need to go thru that process...

  • Build.xml - this is technically a part of the plugin update but you need to actually accept changes that we make to the build.xml to get some functionality. On occasion a new feature (e.g. the new GUI builder) needs to update the build.xml code but this will only happen if you go into project properties, click OK and accept the prompt to update the build.xml (if such an update exists).

  • Client libraries - these are the API's you use when writing Codename One code (typically CodenameOne.jar and related ports). We usually issue an update to those once every 3-5 weeks together with the plugin update. The plugin ships with these but they are only applied to new projects... When you send a build we implicitly update your libraries to the latest version using a separate update process, you can also use "Update Client Libs" within the Codename One preference to update these manually without sending a build.

  • Device libraries - when you send a build to the servers we use the latest version of the client libraries that might be newer than what you see in the client libs but might not be the latest git master. This allows us to rapidly deploy & test device fixes. This also allows you to work with the code and use newer features that weren't pushed to the Client Libraries. The process of updating the servers is a bit adhoc so there is some opacity around that, we are looking at making this more transparent.

  • VM & builders - The builder code and VM relate to the server side scripts that generate the code. When you have a compilation error on the servers or need an enhancement there we need to deploy it in a process similar to the device libraries deployment.

  • Certificate wizard update - this tool is updated in a completely separate update process despite shipping in the plugin. We had a lot of concerns about Apple changing things suddenly when initially creating this so we decided to allow this to update instantly.

Q: Can I use Kotlin with Codename One? A:

Yes. Kotlin is a first-class option in current Codename One Maven projects. The simplest route is to select Kotlin in Codename One Initializr. The generated project uses the official Kotlin Maven plugin and Kotlin standard library, and Java and Kotlin sources can be mixed in the same application.

The old IntelliJ-only plugin, Kotlin cn1lib and Ant-instrumentation instructions no longer apply. The normal Codename One portability limits still apply: code must use APIs available on the targeted Codename One runtimes, and unrestricted runtime reflection is not supported.

Q: ERROR ITMS-90168: "The binary you uploaded was invalid." A:

Application Loader is no longer the current upload workflow. Codename One Build servers now support direct appstore submission. If you choose to do this manually you can still upload an App Store-signed release build using Transporter, Xcode, or Apple’s supported command-line upload tooling.

ITMS-90168 is a wrapper error, so the important information is the detailed delivery log beneath it. The relevant message was “The resulting API analysis file is too large.”

  • Rebuild with a current Codename One release and current build servers.

  • Confirm that this is an iOS release/App Store build, not a development build. Verify that the distribution certificate, provisioning profile and bundle identifier match.

  • Increment the build number and upload using current Transporter.

  • If Apple still rejects it, retain the Transporter delivery log and the Codename One build ID; those are required to distinguish an Apple processing failure from a signing or generated-binary problem.

  • Re-running the certificate wizard is not a generic fix and can create additional signing mismatches if existing certificates are revoked unnecessarily.
